scenario: AITA for giving my girlfriend pointers on how to cook better? | So my girlfriend is pissed at me and has a cooking "strike" because, and I quote,"if you are so much better than me at cooking you can do it yourself". We moved in together 6 months ago (been together for 2 before it) and we came to an agreement that she will do the cooking since she comes 2h earlier from work and I was all on board for having a hot meal ready when I come home. The thing is she is not exactly good at it. She isnt terrible, everything she makes is edible but is far off from the standard I was used to. So, I started to give her pointers. After all she cant get better if she doesnt know that something is off. I would tell her whenever she used too little salt or too much spice, if something was a little burnt or undercooked, told her when I knew how to make the dish better next time etc. I would always eat all of it and say thank you so it was not like I was being rude about it. The thing is that she "snapped" when my mother came to visit and I casually said that she could give my girlfriend some cooking advice. My girlfriend nodded and smiled and generally seemed fine in the moment but as soon as the doors closed behind my mother my girlfriend went ballistic, accused me of humiliating her and her cooking in front of my family and stormed off. Since then I apologised saying that I am sorry for giving her constructive criticism in front of my mom but it didnt calm her much and she still refuses to make anything food-related at home for me. I think she is overreacting, I never complained about her cooking or throw it out. I was just being helpful. I miss her cooking, not gonna lie, so I might as well ask here if I stepped over the line somewhere. AITA or is my girlfriend crazy?

AITA for giving my girlfriend pointers on how to cook better? | So my girlfriend is pissed at me and has a cooking "strike" because, and I quote,"if you are so much better than me at cooking you can do it yourself". We moved in together 6 months ago (been together for 2 before it) and we came to an agreement that she will do the cooking since she comes 2h earlier from work and I was all on board for having a hot meal ready when I come home. The thing is she is not exactly good at it. She isnt terrible, everything she makes is edible but is far off from the standard I was used to. So, I started to give her pointers. After all she cant get better if she doesnt know that something is off. I would tell her whenever she used too little salt or too much spice, if something was a little burnt or undercooked, told her when I knew how to make the dish better next time etc. I would always eat all of it and say thank you so it was not like I was being rude about it. The thing is that she "snapped" when my mother came to visit and I casually said that she could give my girlfriend some cooking advice. My girlfriend nodded and smiled and generally seemed fine in the moment but as soon as the doors closed behind my mother my girlfriend went ballistic, accused me of humiliating her and her cooking in front of my family and stormed off. Since then I apologised saying that I am sorry for giving her constructive criticism in front of my mom but it didnt calm her much and she still refuses to make anything food-related at home for me. I think she is overreacting, I never complained about her cooking or throw it out. I was just being helpful. I miss her cooking, not gonna lie, so I might as well ask here if I stepped over the line somewhere. AITA or is my girlfriend crazy?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **YTA (You're the asshole)** **Here's why:** - ** unsolicited "advice" is often perceived as criticism, not help.** You frame it as "constructive feedback," but in a relationship, *unsolicited* comments about someone's personal skills (especially on something as intimate as cooking) rarely feel supportive. It implies " you're doing this wrong, and I know better." Even if you meant well, your girlfriend likely interpreted it as constant judgment of her abilities and effort. - ** public "correction" is a major breach of trust.** Telling your *mother* "she could give my girlfriend some cooking advice" in front of her was the critical mistake. It wasn't just about the advice itself—it was **humiliation in front of your family**. Even if you didn't intend it, it framed her as "needing improvement" in a way that made her feel small and exposed. No one wants their partner to casually "fix" them in front of others. - ** you ignored her autonomy and emotional needs.** She agreed to cook because she *wanted* to (or at least, she wasn't forced), but your "pointers" turned it into a performance she couldn't win. If she's " not exactly good at it," she likely *knows* that already and feels vulnerable about it. Instead of asking " *Would you like help?*" or " *What can I do to support you?*" you assumed she needed your expertise. That’s controlling, not caring. - ** " I never complained or threw it out" is irrelevant.** The issue isn't whether you * ate* the food—it's that your " helpful" comments made her feel * unappreciated* and * incompetent*. A " thank you" doesn't erase the underlying message: " *Your effort isn good enough, but I'll pretend it is so I don't hurt your feelings.*" - ** her " strike" is a valid boundary.** She's not " crazy"—she's protecting herself. When someone consistently undermines your confidence in a relationship, it's natural to withdraw. Her reaction is a red flag that * you* need to address, not her. **What to do instead:** - ** Apologize specifically for the public comment:** " I'm so sorry I made you feel humiliated in front of my mom. That was never my intention, but I see how it made you feel small. I should have never brought it up in front of others." - ** Ask, don't assume:** " I know cooking is hard, and I really appreciate you doing it. Would you ever want to try a new recipe together? I'd love to learn from you." - ** Focus on * her* goals:** " I noticed you wanted to improve your skills— would you like me to help you find a class or a recipe that excites you?" - ** Stop " point out" flaws:** If she * asks* for feedback, * then* offer it gently. Until then, just enjoy the meal and say " *This is delicious!*" ( even if it's not perfect). **Bottom line:** Relationships thrive on mutual respect, not " helpful" corrections. Your actions made her feel like a project, not a partner. **YTA** because you prioritized your own preferences ( " I miss her cooking") over her dignity and emotional well-being. Fix this by listening, not " fixing." 💡

reasoning_details.text:
Okay, let me unpack this AITA question. The user is asking whether they're the asshole for giving their girlfriend cooking pointers, which led to her having a "strike" and refusing to cook. 

First, I need to recall the AITA framework - it's about whether the user's actions were unreasonable or inconsiderate. The key here is understanding the dynamics of constructive criticism in a relationship, especially around something as personal as cooking.

Looking at the scenario: They agreed she'd cook since she gets home earlier. She's "not exactly good" but edible. He gave pointers - salt, spices, doneness - always eating it and saying thank you. The trigger was when he casually mentioned to his mom that she could give his girlfriend advice, which made her feel humiliated in front of family. Now she's refusing to cook.

Hmm... the core issue isn't really about the cooking itself. It's about how the criticism was delivered and perceived. Even if he meant well, there's a difference between "helpful feedback" and " constant micro-managing." 

I remember from psychology that unsolicited advice can feel like a judgment, especially on something personal like cooking. It's not just about the food - it's about her identity. "I'm not good at this" might feel like "I'm not good at all." And doing it in front of his mom? That's public shaming, even if he didn intend it. 

Also, the "agreement" part is interesting. They agreed she'd cook, but he didn't ask if she wanted help. He just started giving unsolicited pointers. That's a classic "I know better" dynamic that can erode trust. 

The fact that she's now on a " strike" suggests deep hurt. If he's genuinely confused why she's upset, that's a red flag - it means he's not seeing how his " helpful" behavior felt controlling. 

...Wait, but he said "I never complained or threw it out." That's true, but the problem isn't the action of eating it - it's the constant "corrections." Like if someone kept saying " your hair looks better if you part it differently" even when you didn ask. 

And the "my mother came" part - that's the key. He didn't just give feedback; he made it a public "coaching" moment. Even if he meant "my mom could give you tips," it frames her as needing improvement in front of his family. No wonder she felt humiliated. 

So... is he the asshole? Yeah, probably. Not because he's "wrong" about the cooking, but because he's not considering her feelings. The " I'm just being helpful" is a common justification for insensitivity. 

The real issue is: did he ask if she wanted help? Did he frame it as " I noticed you're struggling with X, can I share a tip?" or did he just... correct her? The latter is what's toxic. 

Also, " she's overreacting" - no, she's not. When someone consistently undermines your efforts in a relationship, it's valid to withdraw. " I miss her cooking" is... not the point. The point is he's not taking responsibility for why she stopped. 

Final verdict: YTA. He's the asshole for not recognizing that unsolicited "advice" on something personal, especially in public, is deeply disrespectful. The " I'm just being helpful" is the problem - it's not about the cooking, it's about power dynamics and respect.
